opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, especially now that the models can write a surprising amount of working code on their own. My take is that programming is less about typing syntax and more about a way of thinking. When you learn to program, you learn to break a fuzzy problem into precise pieces, to reason about what the system is actually doing versus what you hoped it would do, and to debug when those two things diverge. That skill doesn't go away just because a model is generating the lines for you. If anything, it becomes more important.

When you're building with AI models, the hard part is rarely getting the first version working. Anyone can get a demo going in an afternoon. The hard part is taking it from something that works 80% of the time to something you'd put in front of real users. That last stretch is all about understanding failure modes: why did the model do this, is it the prompt, the retrieval, the data, some edge case in the glue code? If you can't read and reason about the code and the system around the model, you're stuck poking at it blindly.

There's also a practical piece. Models are great at generating code, but they're not great at knowing what you actually want, and they'll confidently produce something that looks right and isn't. If you can't evaluate that output, you can't really trust it, and you definitely can't maintain it six months later when something breaks in production.

So I'd frame it this way: the models raise the floor on what one person can build, but understanding programming is what raises the ceiling. The people who will get the most leverage out of these tools are the ones who know enough to steer them, check them, and fix things when they go sideways.

r001.rationale: The response says programming helps diagnose failures across prompts, retrieval, data, and glue code, but does not clearly claim that understanding lower levels of the machine-learning stack enables that diagnosis.

r002.rationale: It says people who know enough to steer, check, and fix model-generated code get more leverage, while people unable to evaluate the output cannot trust or maintain it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that programming matters more now, not less, but what "programming" means has shifted.

The way I think about it is that the model is a really capable collaborator that can write a lot of code very fast, but it doesn't actually own the outcome. You do. And to own the outcome, you have to be able to do a few things that are fundamentally programming skills. You have to be able to decompose a messy problem into pieces that can actually be built. You have to be able to look at what comes back and know whether it's right, not just whether it runs. And when it breaks, which it will, you need to be able to form a hypothesis about why, go find the evidence, and fix it. None of that goes away because the model is typing the characters.

I'd actually argue the bottleneck has moved from writing code to reading and judging code. If you can't read it, you can't review it, and if you can't review it, you're essentially shipping things you don't understand. That's fine for a weekend prototype. It's a real problem when you're building something people depend on, because the failure modes of AI-generated code tend to be subtle. It's not that the function is missing, it's that the edge case is handled wrong, or there's a quiet performance issue, or the abstraction is going to collapse the first time requirements change.

The other piece is that the people who get the most leverage out of these tools are the ones who already have a mental model of how software works. They know what to ask for, they know when the answer smells wrong, and they know how to scope a task so the model succeeds. Someone without that background will get something working, but they'll plateau quickly, and they'll have a much harder time when things go sideways.

So my advice to people getting into this is: don't skip the fundamentals, but also don't learn them the old way. Use the model as a tutor. Have it explain what it wrote. Ask it why it made a choice. Try to predict what it's going to do before you hit enter. You'll learn a lot faster than any of us did, and you'll end up as the kind of engineer who can actually direct these systems instead of just hoping they work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses debugging software and checking AI-generated code, but does not say that understanding lower levels of the machine-learning stack helps diagnose failures efficiently.

r002.rationale: It says people with a mental model of software know how to direct AI tools and get more leverage, while those without that background plateau sooner and struggle when things go wrong.

astra-6.text:
I think learning to program is still important because building software is about much more than producing code. You have to figure out what problem you’re solving, break it into pieces, and decide whether the thing you built actually works. AI can help you write the implementation, but you still need a way to evaluate what it gives you.

And when something goes wrong, that understanding really matters. Is the model misunderstanding your request? Is there a bug? Is the approach itself wrong? Programming gives you the tools to reason through those questions instead of just asking the model to try again.

So I think the emphasis may shift. Memorizing syntax becomes less valuable, but understanding how software works—and being able to read, test, and debug it—remains incredibly useful. Those skills make you much more effective at building with AI.

r001.rationale: The response says programming helps identify whether a failure comes from the model, a bug, or the overall approach, but it does not say that understanding lower levels of the machine-learning stack helps diagnose failures.

r002.rationale: The response says that people who can read, test, and debug AI-generated implementations are much more effective at building with AI, conveying the criterion’s comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
I think programming is still important because writing code is only one part of building software. You also have to figure out what problem you’re solving, break it into pieces, and decide whether the result actually works. AI can help generate an implementation, but you still need enough understanding to evaluate it and debug it when something goes wrong.

In some ways, that makes programming knowledge more valuable. If you can read code, understand how the pieces fit together, and give the model useful feedback, you can get a lot more out of these tools. So I’d focus less on memorizing syntax and more on learning how to reason about programs and test your assumptions.

r002.rationale: It says that people who can read and understand code and give the model useful feedback can get more out of AI tools, communicating an advantage in AI-assisted coding.
